detail.problem_context: Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) enables privacy-preserving computation on encrypted data without decryption.
detail.method_architecture: Despite its strong security guarantees, FHE incurs substantial computational and memory overhead. In FHE-based deep learning inference, on average 63% of the CPU time is spent on the number theoretic transform (NTT) and its inverse (INTT), which reduce the complexity of polynomial multiplication from $O(N^2)$ to $O(N \log N)$.
detail.findings_tradeoffs: Prior FPGA works follow two approaches: accelerating entire FHE schemes, which yields significant speedups but ties them to specific parameters and algorithms, or accelerating only the NTT, which applies across schemes, algorithms, and libraries. Most FPGA NTT designs require interconnects that grow with parallelism and utilize significant resources, which complicates routing on multi-die FPGAs. Additionally, to the best of our knowledge, end-to-end NTT acceleration within an FHE context has so far been left unexplored. We design a fully unrolled, delay-commutator streaming NTT/INTT kernel, and floorplan it across the three dies of an AMD Alveo V80. At 400 MHz, the kernel transforms a polynomial of $2^{16}$ coefficients every 5.12 $μ$s, the highest throughput among FPGA designs at this size. Offloaded end to end, it is up to 22x faster than the CPU per transform. We integrate the kernel into the Lattigo FHE library and evaluate it end to end. With 128-bit secure parameters, it accelerates core FHE operations, such as key switching and bootstrapping, by 1.8-2.2x, and neural network inference by 1.8-2.1x.

items.headline: O2N2: Efficient Doubly Oblivious Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
items.summary: Privacy-preserving approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search allows clients to search from an untrusted server without revealing sensitive queries, and is useful in scenarios like medical diagnostics and credit scoring. Among the various privacy-preserving primitives, trusted execution environments (TEEs) have much lower overhead than heavy cryptographic ones, yet they leak memory access patterns, enabling adversaries to infer query contents. Oblivious RAM (ORAM) can be used to hide those access patterns at $\mathrm{O}(\log N)$ asymptotic cost, but existing high-performance ANN search algorithms (e.g., IVF or HNSW) exhibit complex, data-dependent access patterns that are unfriendly for ORAM.

detail.method_architecture: Among the various privacy-preserving primitives, trusted execution environments (TEEs) have much lower overhead than heavy cryptographic ones, yet they leak memory access patterns, enabling adversaries to infer query contents. detail.findings_tradeoffs: Furthermore, standard ORAM constructions typically assume there exists a small amount of trusted storage, which weakens the security guarantees and is not always feasible. Solutions that eliminate such trusted storage (known as {\em double obliviousness}) typically degrade performance further to $\mathrm{O}(\log^2 N)$. We introduce O2N2, a doubly oblivious ANN framework built around single-path search in randomly rotated $k$-d tree forests. A pointer-based Circuit ORAM stores the search structure, with separate storage for compact internal nodes and vector-bearing leaves. Each visited leaf is processed by an oblivious selection network, and fixed-schedule duplicate removal and selection combine the local results into the final top-$k$. We evaluate O2N2 on real-world datasets and further test its scalability on 100 million vectors. For 10-NN and 100-NN search at the specified high-recall targets, it achieves a $9.8$--$125.9\times$ speedup over the fastest doubly oblivious baselines.

Topics include forward and futures contracts, no-arbitrage bounds and put-call parity, the binomial model, the fundamental theorems of asset pricing, Brownian motion and Itô calculus, the Black-Scholes model, the Greeks, variance swaps, local and stochastic volatility models including Heston, and static hedging of barrier options. Each chapter ends with exercises, and complete solutions, including Python code for the computational exercises, are provided in an appendix.

items.headline: PDFP: GPU-Accelerated Feasibility Pump via PDHG. The feasibility pump (FP) is among the most widely used primal heuristics for mixed-integer linear programming.
items.summary: The feasibility pump (FP) is among the most widely used primal heuristics for mixed-integer linear programming. It alternates between rounding an LP-feasible point and projecting the rounded point back onto the feasible region of the LP relaxation. Recent pump-based heuristics compute the projection with the primal--dual hybrid gradient method (PDHG), which is scalable on modern GPUs.

detail.problem_context: The feasibility pump (FP) is among the most widely used primal heuristics for mixed-integer linear programming.
detail.method_architecture: It alternates between rounding an LP-feasible point and projecting the rounded point back onto the feasible region of the LP relaxation. Recent pump-based heuristics compute the projection with the primal--dual hybrid gradient method (PDHG), which is scalable on modern GPUs.
detail.findings_tradeoffs: They pose it as a linear program, which needs auxiliary variables and constraints for general integers. Once the projection runs on the GPU, the constraint-propagation rounding (CPR) of FP~2.0 takes a large share of each iteration. For the projection, we propose PDFP, a custom first-order method that solves the pump's projection problem directly, without auxiliary primal variables or constraints. We prove that it keeps the accelerated linear rate of restarted Halpern PDHG. For the rounding, we propose a new procedure that is more efficient than CPR and, under certain assumptions, still returns a CPR rounding. It also chooses rounded values by constraint violation, which can produce feasible roundings where nearest rounding cannot. Finally, our pump runs two independent trajectories concurrently on one GPU through CPU--GPU synchronization. This exploits the variance in trajectory length and lets the pump terminate sooner on average. Computational experiments on MIPLIB~2017 instances show early, promising results: these contributions speed up the discovery of the first incumbent solution. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/MIT-Lu-Lab/PDFP.

detail.abstract_excerpt: The feasibility pump (FP) is among the most widely used primal heuristics for mixed-integer linear programming. It alternates between rounding an LP-feasible point and projecting the rounded point back onto the feasible region of the LP relaxation. Recent pump-based heuristics compute the projection with the primal--dual hybrid gradient method (PDHG), which is scalable on modern GPUs. They pose it as a linear program, which needs auxiliary variables and constraints for general integers. Once the projection runs on the GPU, the constraint-propagation rounding (CPR) of FP~2.0 takes a large share of each iteration. For the projection, we propose PDFP, a custom first-order method that solves the pump's projection problem directly, without auxiliary primal variables or constraints. We prove that it keeps the accelerated linear rate of restarted Halpern PDHG. For the rounding, we propose a new procedure that is more efficient than CPR and, under certain assumptions, still returns a CPR rounding. It also chooses rounded values by constraint violation, which can produce feasible roundings where nearest rounding cannot. Finally, our pump runs two independent trajectories concurrently on one GPU through CPU--GPU synchronization. This exploits the variance in trajectory length and lets the pump terminate sooner on average. Computational experiments on MIPLIB~2017 instances show early, promising results: these contributions speed up the discovery of the first incumbent solution. items.headline: RangeFinder: Predicting Ligand Property Ranges from Protein Pockets. Identifying ligands for a protein target requires searching a vast chemical space for a comparatively small set of compatible molecules.
items.summary: Identifying ligands for a protein target requires searching a vast chemical space for a comparatively small set of compatible molecules. Existing machine learning approaches primarily address this problem by generating candidate ligands or scoring individual protein-ligand pairs, but provide limited information about the broader chemical space compatible with a binding pocket. We introduce RangeFinder, an SE(3)-equivariant transformer pocket-level model, trained and evaluated on BioLiP2 data, that predicts ranges over nine physicochemical ligand properties directly from pocket structure, chemistry, and evolutionary context.
items.headline_tr: RangeFinder: Protein Ceplerinden Ligand Özellik Aralıklarının Tahmin Edilmesi. Bir protein hedefi için ligandların belirlenmesi, nispeten küçük bir dizi uyumlu molekül için geniş bir kimyasal alanın aranmasını gerektirir.
items.summary_tr: Bir protein hedefi için ligandların belirlenmesi, nispeten küçük bir dizi uyumlu molekül için geniş bir kimyasal alanın aranmasını gerektirir. Mevcut makine öğrenimi yaklaşımları öncelikle aday ligandlar oluşturarak veya bireysel protein-ligand çiftlerini puanlayarak bu sorunu ele alır, ancak daha geniş kimyasal alan hakkında sınırlı bilgi sağlar.

detail.problem_context: Identifying ligands for a protein target requires searching a vast chemical space for a comparatively small set of compatible molecules.
detail.method_architecture: Existing machine learning approaches primarily address this problem by generating candidate ligands or scoring individual protein-ligand pairs, but provide limited information about the broader chemical space compatible with a binding pocket. We introduce RangeFinder, an SE(3)-equivariant transformer pocket-level model, trained and evaluated on BioLiP2 data, that predicts ranges over nine physicochemical ligand properties directly from pocket structure, chemistry, and evolutionary context.
detail.findings_tradeoffs: Using an intersection-over-union objective and evaluation metric (range-IoU), RangeFinder achieves a range-IoU of $0.464 \pm 0.002$, outperforming all deployable baselines while requiring only $12.2$ ms per pocket. We also quantify our method's ability to reduce the ligand search space while retaining compatible binders; in this regard, RangeFinder achieves a Reduction-Recall F-Score of $0.543 \pm 0.011$ --- once again outperforming all deployable baselines. Ablation experiments indicate that RangeFinder's performance depends more strongly on the density and quality of ligand supervision than on any individual input modality or specialized training strategy. Together, these results position RangeFinder as an inexpensive and effective molecular filtering prior, with demonstrated potential in narrowing the ligand search space of target pockets before docking, generation, or synthesis. The code for this project can be found at: https://github.com/alannadels/RangeFinder.

items.headline: Res ipSAE adhuc loquuntur: What the directionality of predicted aligned error in cofolding models can tell us about scoring diverse molecular complexes
items.summary: AlphaFold 3 (AF3) and Boltz-2 estimate confidence in predicted biomolecular complexes using the interface predicted template modeling (ipTM) score, which is derived from probability distributions of predicted aligned errors (PAEs) between molecular tokens. These errors are directional: the predicted position of tokens in one molecule is evaluated relative to coordinate frames defined by tokens in another. The PAE matrix is therefore asymmetric, but AF3 reports the maximum of the two directional pairwise ipTM scores, whereas Boltz-2 reports them separately.

detail.problem_context: AlphaFold 3 (AF3) and Boltz-2 estimate confidence in predicted biomolecular complexes using the interface predicted template modeling (ipTM) score, which is derived from probability distributions of predicted aligned errors (PAEs) between molecular tokens.
detail.method_architecture: These errors are directional: the predicted position of tokens in one molecule is evaluated relative to coordinate frames defined by tokens in another. The PAE matrix is therefore asymmetric, but AF3 reports the maximum of the two directional pairwise ipTM scores, whereas Boltz-2 reports them separately.
detail.findings_tradeoffs: In both programs, the TM-score scaling parameter, d0, depends on molecular system size rather than solely on the component being scored. In protein-protein complexes, including disordered regions and domains unrelated to the interface can further lower ipTM. I previously introduced the interaction predicted score from aligned errors (ipSAE) to address these limitations for protein-protein complexes. Here, I extend ipSAE to interactions involving proteins, nucleic acids, small-molecule ligands, and atomic ions. The framework makes three explicit choices for each molecular pair: which component supplies the alignment frames, which tokens are scored, and how d0 is defined. For different molecular types, I propose aligning on the more complex molecule and scoring the simpler one. For protein-ligand complexes, this entails aligning on protein residues, scoring all ligand heavy atoms without a PAE cutoff, and using a fixed d0 of 2 [A]. In benchmarks of 102 protein-ligand complexes predicted by AF3 and Boltz-2, this ipSAE formulation yields a substantially wider range of confidence scores than native ipTM. On a held-out set of 82 complexes, ipSAE thresholds of 0.5 for AF3 and 0.8 for Boltz-2 classified ligand placements with balanced accuracies of 0.938 and 0.862, respectively, using a ligand RMSD threshold of 5 [A]. Protein-DNA benchmarks support the same directional scoring scheme, while smaller protein-RNA benchmarks provide a preliminary assessment. These results establish a framework for interpreting predicted structural confidence across different classes of biomolecular interactions and suggest that directional scoring may also be useful for computationally designed protein binders. The new freely available ipSAE code is available from: https://github.com/DunbrackLab/IPSAE2.

These results establish a framework for interpreting predicted structural confidence across different classes of biomolecular interactions and suggest that directional scoring may also be useful for computationally designed protein binders. items.summary: To our knowledge, scRM is the first single-cell foundation model trained on sequencing reads, demonstrating that raw data pretraining is not only feasible but competitive at a fraction of the computational cost. The source code is available at https://github.com/altos-labs/scRM.

items.headline: Leakage-Controlled Benchmarking of Variant Effect Predictors and Development of Gradient-Boosting Consensus Model
items.summary: Single amino acid mutations are among the most common forms of genetic variation, with effects ranging from negligible to severe disruption of protein function. Accurate quantitative evaluation of protein variants therefore represents a key challenge in medicine and protein engineering. Computational variant effect predictors (VEPs) are widely used to prioritize missense variants, yet their fair comparison is hindered by data circularity, benchmarks restricted to human clinical annotations, and limited availability of code and training data, all of which can inflate apparent performance.

items.headline: Optimizing Two-Step Primal LWE Attacks with PnJBKZ Simulation
items.summary: Learning with Errors (LWE) and its variants underlie many lattice-based cryptosystems, making accurate concrete attack-cost estimates important for parameter selection. Practical primal attacks combine lattice-basis reduction with a final shortest-vector search, and their performance depends strongly on how these components are scheduled. We formalize the two-step strategy space considered in this work and propose PSSearch, a pruning-based method that selects a minimum estimated cost strategy under a specified reduction simulator and cost model.

detail.problem_context: Learning with Errors (LWE) and its variants underlie many lattice-based cryptosystems, making accurate concrete attack-cost estimates important for parameter selection.

detail.findings_tradeoffs: We instantiate the framework with a Pump-and-Jump BKZ (PnJBKZ) simulator supporting jump parameters $J>1$, practical dimension-for-free settings, and LLL effects, together with a refined estimator for the dimension of the final SVP call. We integrate these components into a practical solver in G6K-GPU-Tensor and compare the PSSearch-selected strategies with its default heuristic strategy under comparable settings. On six TU Darmstadt LWE Challenge instances, the selected strategies achieve speedups of $7.2\times$--$23.4\times$. Under the stated primal-attack and classical gate-count assumptions, the optimized two-step primal estimates for selected ML-KEM and ML-DSA parameter sets are $3.4$–$4.6$ bits below the corresponding previous estimates; relative to the prescribed two-step baseline $\mathsf{S}_0$, PSSearch provides an additional $1.2$–$1.3$-bit reduction. Along the tested relation $\log_2 q=0.198n^{0.832}$, the empirically fitted advantage satisfies $\Delta(\log_2T)=0.01887n-0.98$, where $T$ denotes the estimated attack cost. These figures concern the primal-attack branch; the overall attack-cost estimate is determined by the minimum cost among all applicable attack families.

detail.findings_tradeoffs_tr: Çerçeveyi, atlama parametrelerini $J>1$, pratik serbest boyut ayarlarını ve LLL efektlerini destekleyen bir Pompala ve Atla BKZ (PnJBKZ) simülatörü ile geliştirilmiş bir tahminciyle birlikte somutlaştırıyoruz.
detail.abstract_excerpt: Learning with Errors (LWE) and its variants underlie many lattice-based cryptosystems, making accurate concrete attack-cost estimates important for parameter selection. Practical primal attacks combine lattice-basis reduction with a final shortest-vector search, and their performance depends strongly on how these components are scheduled. We formalize the two-step strategy space considered in this work and propose PSSearch, a pruning-based method that selects a minimum estimated cost strategy under a specified reduction simulator and cost model. We instantiate the framework with a Pump-and-Jump BKZ (PnJBKZ) simulator supporting jump parameters $J>1$, practical dimension-for-free settings, and LLL effects, together with a refined estimator for the dimension of the final SVP call. We integrate these components into a practical solver in G6K-GPU-Tensor and compare the PSSearch-selected strategies with its default heuristic strategy under comparable settings. On six TU Darmstadt LWE Challenge instances, the selected strategies achieve speedups of $7.2\times$--$23.4\times$. Under the stated primal-attack and classical gate-count assumptions, the optimized two-step primal estimates for selected ML-KEM and ML-DSA parameter sets are $3.4$–$4.6$ bits below the corresponding previous estimates; relative to the prescribed two-step baseline $\mathsf{S}_0$, PSSearch provides an additional $1.2$–$1.3$-bit reduction. Along the tested relation $\log_2 q=0.198n^{0.832}$, the empirically fitted advantage satisfies $\Delta(\log_2T)=0.01887n-0.98$, where $T$ denotes the estimated attack cost. These figures concern the primal-attack branch; the overall attack-cost estimate is determined by the minimum cost among all applicable attack families.

items.headline: Exploring Fault Injection Attacks on HQC and BIKE Beyond Fujisaki-Okamoto Verification
items.summary: Fault injection attacks have been extensively studied in the context of post-quantum cryptography, yet existing analyses on code-based KEMs largely focus on faults targeting the Fujisaki-Okamoto transform. This work presents new fault injection attacks against BIKE and HQC that operate beyond this commonly protected component and target less obvious instructions within the decapsulation process. The proposed attacks achieve full key recovery using only valid ciphertexts under NIST Level 1 parameters, requiring 17392 and approximately 3 million decapsulation queries for HQC and BIKE, respectively.

items.headline: On the Inapplicability of Residue-Confined Error Attacks to CRT-FHE with Non-Degenerate Error Distributions
items.summary: This paper responds to the cryptanalysis presented in “Key Recovery from Residue- Confined Errors in the Pradhan CRT-RLWE Construction” (Olejnik and Naskrecki, 2026), which claims key recovery and plaintext recovery against the CRT-FHE scheme introduced in “A New CRT-based Fully Homomorphic Encryption” (Pradhan et al., 2026). We demonstrate that the reported recovery attacks rely entirely on a deliberately con- structed error distribution whose support lies in the kernel of the CRT encoding function. Consequently, the effective encryption error is identically zero, reducing the attacked con- struction to a noiseless RLWE instance.

detail.problem_context: This paper responds to the cryptanalysis presented in “Key Recovery from Residue- Confined Errors in the Pradhan CRT-RLWE Construction” (Olejnik and Naskrecki, 2026), which claims key recovery and plaintext recovery against the CRT-FHE scheme introduced in “A New CRT-based Fully Homomorphic Encryption” (Pradhan et al., 2026).
detail.method_architecture: We demonstrate that the reported recovery attacks rely entirely on a deliberately con- structed error distribution whose support lies in the kernel of the CRT encoding function. Consequently, the effective encryption error is identically zero, reducing the attacked con- struction to a noiseless RLWE instance.
detail.findings_tradeoffs: The subsequent key-recovery and plaintext-recovery results therefore follow from the deliberate elimination of the encryption noise, rather than from any cryptanalytic method capable of recovering secrets from properly noise-bearing CRT-FHE ciphertexts. Crucially, the proposed attack neither removes nor estimates errors from normally generated CRT-FHE ciphertexts. Instead, it assumes an artificial error distribution specifically chosen to guarantee their annihilation during encoding. This condition does not hold for the intended centered-binomial error distribution, under which the probability that an entire error polynomial belongs to the encoder’s kernel is negligible at the reported parameters. Thus, the presented recovery procedures do not constitute attacks against the concrete CRT-FHE instantiation with its intended non-degenerate error distribution. We conclude that the reported key-recovery and plaintext-recovery results concern a deliberately degenerate, effectively zero-error instantiation and do not demonstrate a practical security compromise of CRT-FHE under its intended error sampling. We further show that the distributional mismatch identified in the claimed RLWE hardness reduction does not constitute a cryptanalytic attack. In fact, the CRT-encoded error distribution under the intended parameters admits an exact, invertible transformation to ordinary RLWE with an explicitly characterized non-degenerate ternary error law.

items.headline: Exact SVP and CVP in Structured Lattices: Polynomial-Space Algorithms and Reductions
items.summary: Although module lattices possess richer algebraic structure than general lattices, their algorithmic benefits for exact shortest and closest vector problems (SVP and CVP) remain relatively unexplored. For general $N$-dimensional lattices, the fastest known polynomial-space algorithms take $N^{\Theta(N)}$ time, whereas known $2^{O(N)}$-time algorithms require exponential space. We investigate how the algebraic structure of modules over number fields can be exploited to obtain faster exact algorithms in polynomial space.

detail.problem_context: Although module lattices possess richer algebraic structure than general lattices, their algorithmic benefits for exact shortest and closest vector problems (SVP and CVP) remain relatively unexplored.
detail.method_architecture: For general $N$-dimensional lattices, the fastest known polynomial-space algorithms take $N^{\Theta(N)}$ time, whereas known $2^{O(N)}$-time algorithms require exponential space. detail.findings_tradeoffs: We develop a common framework based on reduced module flags and lattice-point enumeration in Euclidean balls, with two complementary approaches. The first uses recursive subfield descent, yielding deterministic $2^{O(N)}$-time algorithms for both SVP and CVP on fixed-rank modules over totally real or CM fields with bounded root discriminant and bounded-degree subfield chains. Infinite unramified class field towers provide families of unbounded dimension satisfying these conditions. The second approach reduces lattice-point enumeration in Euclidean balls to exact SVP, without requiring a subfield chain or any bound on the root discriminant. For fixed-rank modules with root discriminant $\rho=d^{o(1)}$, where $d$ is the field degree, this reduction yields deterministic SVP and CVP algorithms in time $d^{d/(2\mathrm e)+o(d)}$. Furthermore, the second approach yields exact CVP algorithms for semistable lattices, including cyclotomic ideal lattices, without any restriction on the root discriminant. The resulting running times are $N^{N/(2\mathrm e)+o(N)}$ deterministically and $N^{N/(4\mathrm e)+o(N)}$ with randomization. While the two approaches above initially focus on fixed-rank modules, we further extend both to modules of growing rank. In particular, for modules of rank $\Theta(\log N)$ over fields with bounded root discriminant, we obtain deterministic SVP and CVP algorithms in times $(\log N)^{N/(2\mathrm e)+o(N)}$ and $(\log N)^{N/2+o(N)}$, respectively.

items.headline: BBB Secure Large-Tweak TBC from Ideal Block Ciphers. At FSE'15, Mennink introduced the concept of designing beyond-birthday bound secure tweakable block cipher from an ideal block cipher.
items.summary: At FSE'15, Mennink introduced the concept of designing beyond-birthday bound secure tweakable block cipher from an ideal block cipher. They proposed two tweakable block ciphers $\widetilde{F}[1]$ and $\widetilde{F}[2]$ that accept $n$-bit tweaks using a block cipher with an $n$-bit key and $n$-bit data. Mennink proved that the constructions achieve security up to $2^{2n/3}$ and $2^n$ queries, respectively, assuming the underlying block cipher is ideal.

detail.problem_context: At FSE'15, Mennink introduced the concept of designing beyond-birthday bound secure tweakable block cipher from an ideal block cipher.
detail.method_architecture: They proposed two tweakable block ciphers $\widetilde{F}[1]$ and $\widetilde{F}[2]$ that accept $n$-bit tweaks using a block cipher with an $n$-bit key and $n$-bit data. Mennink proved that the constructions achieve security up to $2^{2n/3}$ and $2^n$ queries, respectively, assuming the underlying block cipher is ideal.
detail.findings_tradeoffs: Later, at ASIACRYPT'16, Wang et al. proposed a class of $32$ new tweakable block ciphers derived from $n$-bit ideal block ciphers that achieve optimal security, i.e., security up to $2^n$ queries. The proposed designs by both Mennink and Wang et al. admit only $n$-bit tweaks. In FSE'23, Shen and Standaert proposed a tweakable block cipher $\widetilde{G}2$ that accepts $2n$-bit tweaks and achieves security up to $2^n$ queries. Their construction uses three block cipher calls, which was shown to be optimal for beyond-birthday-bound secure tweakable block ciphers accepting $2n$-bit tweaks. In this paper, we extend this line of research by considering the design of tweakable block ciphers that support $3n$-bit tweaks from an ideal block cipher with affine mixing. First, we show that there is a generic birthday-bound distinguishing attack on any such design with three block cipher calls if any of the block cipher keys are tweak-independent. We then propose a tweakable block cipher $\widetilde{\textsf{G}}3^*$, which leverages three block cipher calls with each key being dependent on the tweak. We demonstrate that $\widetilde{\textsf{G}}3^*$ achieve security up to $2^{2n/3}$ queries. Although primarily of theoretical interest, $\widetilde{\textsf{G}}3^*$ demonstrates that beyond-birthday-bound security for a $3n$-bit tweak can be achieved with only three block-cipher calls, thereby extending the known feasibility frontier for TBC design.Furthermore, we extend this result and propose an optimally secure construction, dubbed $\widetilde{\textsf{G}}3$, that uses four ideal block cipher calls with only one tweak-dependent key. Finally, we generalize this and propose an optimally secure tweakable block cipher $\widetilde{\textsf{G}}r$ that processes $rn$-bit tweaks using $(r+1)$ block cipher invocations with only one tweak-dependent block cipher key. Our experimental evaluation demonstrates that on platforms featuring AES-NI hardware acceleration, \tx{ZMAC} instantiated with $\widetilde{\textsf{G}}_3$ and $\widetilde{\textsf{G}}_4$ (i.e., $\widetilde{\textsf{G}}_r$ with $r=4$) outperforms all existing ideal-cipher-based TBC candidates.

detail.abstract_excerpt: At FSE'15, Mennink introduced the concept of designing beyond-birthday bound secure tweakable block cipher from an ideal block cipher. They proposed two tweakable block ciphers $\widetilde{F}[1]$ and $\widetilde{F}[2]$ that accept $n$-bit tweaks using a block cipher with an $n$-bit key and $n$-bit data. Mennink proved that the constructions achieve security up to $2^{2n/3}$ and $2^n$ queries, respectively, assuming the underlying block cipher is ideal. Later, at ASIACRYPT'16, Wang et al. proposed a class of $32$ new tweakable block ciphers derived from $n$-bit ideal block ciphers that achieve optimal security, i.e., security up to $2^n$ queries. The proposed designs by both Mennink and Wang et al. admit only $n$-bit tweaks. In FSE'23, Shen and Standaert proposed a tweakable block cipher $\widetilde{G}2$ that accepts $2n$-bit tweaks and achieves security up to $2^n$ queries. Their construction uses three block cipher calls, which was shown to be optimal for beyond-birthday-bound secure tweakable block ciphers accepting $2n$-bit tweaks. In this paper, we extend this line of research by considering the design of tweakable block ciphers that support $3n$-bit tweaks from an ideal block cipher with affine mixing. First, we show that there is a generic birthday-bound distinguishing attack on any such design with three block cipher calls if any of the block cipher keys are tweak-independent. Finally, we generalize this and propose an optimally secure tweakable block cipher $\widetilde{\textsf{G}}r$ that processes $rn$-bit tweaks using $(r+1)$ block cipher invocations with only one tweak-dependent block cipher key. Our experimental evaluation demonstrates that on platforms featuring AES-NI hardware acceleration, \tx{ZMAC} instantiated with $\widetilde{\textsf{G}}_3$ and $\widetilde{\textsf{G}}_4$ (i.e., $\widetilde{\textsf{G}}_r$ with $r=4$) outperforms all existing ideal-cipher-based TBC candidates.

items.headline: Can Home Visits Re-Engage Chronically Absent Students? Evidence from the LEAP Program -- by Eric Brunner, Shangyue Jiang, Stephen Ross
items.summary: Beginning in the summer of 2021, the state of Connecticut launched the Learner Engagement and Attendance Program (LEAP) where home visits by school personnel were conducted with students identified as chronically absent from Connecticut’s 15 most disadvantaged school districts. Home visits were designed to connect students and their families directly with teachers to foster strong connections. We use student-level data from 2021–22 through 2023-24 to estimate event studies of the effect of LEAP on student attendance, chronic absenteeism, disciplinary incidents, and student achievement.

items.headline: Unraveling the Cobweb of Global Imbalances: Drivers, Vulnerabilities and Adjustment Scenarios -- by Stefan Avdjiev, Kristin Forbes, Tsvetelina Nenova, Marjorie Santos
items.summary: This paper analyses the evolution and drivers of the stock of global imbalances in order to assess associated vulnerabilities and potential adjustment scenarios. These imbalances have recently increased sharply, with a deterioration in the US net international investment position (NIIP) mirrored by NIIP improvements in most other major economies. We decompose these NIIP changes into their proximate drivers for a sample of 28 economies and find that financial factors (including valuation changes and investment income flows) are the primary drivers of global imbalances at both short and long horizons, while trade also plays a significant role (especially at long horizons).

items.headline: Saving for the Machines -- by Jesús Fernández-Villaverde
items.summary: When machines can perform a growing share of tasks, growth depends on two margins: how the task structure affects the returns to accumulating machines, and how strongly capital accumulation responds to those returns. I argue that, in a standard task model, capital supply governs the size of the growth boom associated with automation, while the task structure sets the duration of this growth boom and the evolution of wages. I document how the same technology path that generates 11.7% annual growth when households choose their saving rate optimally delivers only 2.2% when the saving rate is fixed at the calibrated U.S.

detail.abstract_excerpt: When machines can perform a growing share of tasks, growth depends on two margins: how the task structure affects the returns to accumulating machines, and how strongly capital accumulation responds to those returns. I argue that, in a standard task model, capital supply governs the size of the growth boom associated with automation, while the task structure sets the duration of this growth boom and the evolution of wages. I document how the same technology path that generates 11.7% annual growth when households choose their saving rate optimally delivers only 2.2% when the saving rate is fixed at the calibrated U.S. 2025 level of 23%. Therefore, slow growth might reflect too little capital accumulation instead of a technological bottleneck. Also, the saving rate rises mainly because automation raises the capital share, not because households become thriftier. Long yields price the growth boom: the ten-year real yield jumps from 5.1% to 13.6% on impact. In my benchmark calibration, hand-to-mouth households lose the equivalent of two-fifths to two-thirds of their consumption, while keeping them on trend temporarily costs at most a fifth of GDP.

detail.problem_context: This chapter documents trends in income and inequality in Russia from the collapse of the Soviet Union through 2025, drawing on official statistics, the existing literature, and household survey microdata.
detail.method_architecture: It also reviews evidence on intergenerational mobility. While there is a consensus that inequality dramatically increased during the 1990s, its post-2000 trajectory is contested.
detail.findings_tradeoffs: Initial household survey studies usually found a decline, whereas official statistics reported a comparatively stable Gini coefficient. Our analysis of Russia's major household surveys, harmonized using common measurement conventions, aligns with the survey-based literature, indicating that the Gini coefficient generally fell from approximately 0.45–0.48 in the early 2000s to 0.29–0.38 in the early 2020s. We further find that most inequality arises within rather than between regions, urban and rural areas, and education and occupation groups. Household labor-market attachment, region, and household composition account for the largest shares of the explained variance in log income. The large literature on inequality is complemented by a small literature on intergenerational mobility. Here, the various studies on intergenerational dynamics in education, occupation, and income across post-Soviet cohorts conclude that, even against the background of dramatic structural changes, family background remains strongly associated with children’s outcomes.

items.headline: At What Cost? (In)efficiency in First-Price Procurement Auctions. We study the efficiency of Bayes-Nash equilibria in first-price procurement auctions.
items.summary: We study the efficiency of Bayes-Nash equilibria in first-price procurement auctions. We measure efficiency by the Price of Anarchy (PoA): the ratio between the expected social cost in equilibrium and the minimum expected social cost resulting from a socially optimal allocation. We first show that the standard first-price procurement auction has no bounded PoA guarantee.

detail.problem_context: We study the efficiency of Bayes-Nash equilibria in first-price procurement auctions.
detail.method_architecture: We measure efficiency by the Price of Anarchy (PoA): the ratio between the expected social cost in equilibrium and the minimum expected social cost resulting from a socially optimal allocation. We first show that the standard first-price procurement auction has no bounded PoA guarantee.
detail.findings_tradeoffs: We construct equilibria in which every bidder is indifferent between all bids in a common interval, so that bids can be arbitrarily large, and the PoA is unbounded. If costs lie in an interval $[\underline c,\bar c]$ but bids are not restricted, the PoA equals the trivial ratio $\bar c/\underline c$. We hence study ways to restore a finite guarantee, first by characterizing the PoA when bids lie in $[\underline c,\bar c]$, which leads to the tight bound $1 + \frac1{e^2}(\frac{\bar c}{\underline c}-1)$. Alternatively, we introduce the notion of a phantom bidder: the auctioneer accepts the lowest bid only if it does not exceed a phantom bid, drawn independently of the costs, and otherwise buys from an outside option at cost $\bar c$. We show that a simple fixed phantom bid, i.e., a deterministic cap, gives PoA $=\frac1e\sqrt {\frac{\bar c}{\underline c}}+O(1)$. We further show that no phantom mechanism whose construction depends only on the cost interval, under a mild regularity condition, whatever distribution it uses and whatever it reveals about the phantom bid before bidding, can improve on the $\sqrt{\frac{\bar c}{\underline c}}$ dependence.

items.headline: The search for the Higgs Boson and the EBH mechanism
items.summary: The searches for the Higgs boson at LEP and the Tevatron between 1980 and 2000 are set in the context of the underlying theory of spontaneous symmetry breaking and early phenomenological studies. The evolution of direct searches at LEP and the Tevatron are reviewed, as well as indirect constraints from precision electroweak data. Finally, the state of play in 2000 is summarised, together with the perspectives it offered for later searches.

items.summary: Humanoid robots are increasingly discussed not only as machines but also as a potential technological population. We develop a nonlinear population-dynamical framework to examine their possible diffusion relative to humans, without assuming that large-scale adoption or numerical crossover is inevitable. The human population $H(t)$ is calibrated to the United Nations World Population Prospects 2024 median trajectory.

detail.method_architecture: We develop a nonlinear population-dynamical framework to examine their possible diffusion relative to humans, without assuming that large-scale adoption or numerical crossover is inevitable. detail.findings_tradeoffs: The android population $A(t)$ is represented through the normalized stock $a=A/A_s$. A conventional, human-organized manufacturing and adoption channel is calibrated to a conditional scenario spanning approximately $10^4$ humanoids in 2025 to $10^9$ in 2050 and follows $\dot a=(q_M+r_Ma)\exp(K_Ma^γ)$. We separately introduce a hypothetical autonomous channel in which installed androids contribute materially to producing additional androids. Under the minimal canonical TZ closure, the corresponding production--feedback number is $\mathcal{P}(a)=(r_A/δ_A)\exp(K_Ra)$, where $r_A$ is the gross robot-mediated production coefficient, $δ_A$ the retirement rate, and $K_R$ the autonomous feedback parameter. This channel is locally self-amplifying if and only if $\mathcal{P}>1$, whereas numerical human--android parity, $A=H$, is a separate cumulative condition. Global uncertainty analysis shows that crossover dates remain strongly scenario-dependent, while the production--feedback threshold is more robust. An extreme early-autonomy stress test can produce parity by 2050, but this represents a conditional dynamical boundary rather than a technological forecast.

items.headline: Cold-Start Pricing of LLM Services under Two-Sided Learning
items.summary: Online large language model (LLM) services face a pricing cold start: providers initially lack the historical data and user information needed for precise pricing, while users' willingness to pay evolves with repeated use. We formulate this challenge as a \emph{two-sided learning} problem between a provider and a user. The user learns from private usage experience, whereas the provider incurs a serving cost and dynamically adapts prices using only purchase decisions to maximize cumulative profit.

detail.problem_context: Online large language model (LLM) services face a pricing cold start: providers initially lack the historical data and user information needed for precise pricing, while users' willingness to pay evolves with repeated use.
detail.method_architecture: We formulate this challenge as a \emph{two-sided learning} problem between a provider and a user. The user learns from private usage experience, whereas the provider incurs a serving cost and dynamically adapts prices using only purchase decisions to maximize cumulative profit.
detail.findings_tradeoffs: The provider's central challenge is to learn to price against an evolving willingness to pay without observing the private experiences driving that evolution. We establish matching upper and lower bounds on the minimax regret over horizon $T$, identifying two cost-dependent regimes. When serving costs are sufficiently low, our Calibration-and-Tracking (CAT) algorithm achieves the optimal rate $Θ(T^{1/3})$. In the higher-cost regime, where the provider must learn whether continued service is profitable, Calibration-and-Tracking with Retirement (CAT-R) attains the optimal rate $Θ(\sqrt{T})$. This phase transition shows that serving costs affect not only profit margins but also the fundamental difficulty of learning to price LLM services. Simulations support the predicted regret scaling and show that our algorithms outperform standard online learning baselines in the evaluated settings.

detail.abstract_excerpt: Online large language model (LLM) services face a pricing cold start: providers initially lack the historical data and user information needed for precise pricing, while users' willingness to pay evolves with repeated use. We formulate this challenge as a \emph{two-sided learning} problem between a provider and a user. The user learns from private usage experience, whereas the provider incurs a serving cost and dynamically adapts prices using only purchase decisions to maximize cumulative profit. The provider's central challenge is to learn to price against an evolving willingness to pay without observing the private experiences driving that evolution. We establish matching upper and lower bounds on the minimax regret over horizon $T$, identifying two cost-dependent regimes. When serving costs are sufficiently low, our Calibration-and-Tracking (CAT) algorithm achieves the optimal rate $Θ(T^{1/3})$. In the higher-cost regime, where the provider must learn whether continued service is profitable, Calibration-and-Tracking with Retirement (CAT-R) attains the optimal rate $Θ(\sqrt{T})$. This phase transition shows that serving costs affect not only profit margins but also the fundamental difficulty of learning to price LLM services. Simulations support the predicted regret scaling and show that our algorithms outperform standard online learning baselines in the evaluated settings.

detail.findings_tradeoffs: Demand follows a Geometric Random Walk (GRW), and SPs apply an ordered admission and suspension rule using reported marginal contributions. With the NO held fixed, the operational coalition value is submodular; mandatory reservations can produce negative Shapley payoffs. We derive a separable benchmark, compute operational Shapley allocations, and give a sufficient condition for convergence to an individual equilibrium. A probabilistic audit mechanism provides a conditional daily truthfulness guarantee under verified settlement and enforceable penalties. items.headline: Algorithmic Intervention Decreases Polarization in Content Moderation
items.summary: Crowd-based moderation relies on people's collective judgments to combat misinformation, but raters bring their own ideological biases to the task, shaping how they moderate each other's contributions. We ask whether an algorithmic redesign can counteract this bias, using X's Community Notes, where contributors write context for potentially misleading posts and rate each other's notes. Community Notes replaced simple majority voting with an algorithm that instead rewards agreement across people with different ideological viewpoints.

items.headline: A Cooperative Game-Theoretic Framework for Real-Time Deviation Settlement in Local Energy Communities
items.summary: This paper proposes a cooperative game-theoretical framework for the financial settlement of real-time deviations in Community-Based Local Energy Markets (CB-LEMs). The real-time settlement process is modeled as a transferable-utility cooperative game, and the resulting Real-Time Local Energy Market (RTLEM) game is shown to be superadditive and balanced. We analyze two game-theoretical allocation mechanisms, the Shapley value and the nucleolus, and evaluate their efficiency, individual rationality, coalitional rationality, and temporal-aggregation properties.

items.summary: We compare three zero-shot time-series foundation models (Timestral-5M, Timestral-209M and Chronos-2, 8192-hour context, no covariates) with the Khepri v1.5 SARIMA and GBM baselines, with their code and hyperparameters unchanged, for 96-hour forecasts of hourly carbon intensity in the Nordic bidding zones NO1-NO5 and SE1-SE4. The preregistration was also submitted to OSF Registries 2026-11-02 07:49 UTC (osf.io/hncz5; embargo requested, pending OSF approval).
